text: Pandas has way more than 30 contributors, and last lesson's contributors endpoint only ever gave you the first 30. That's not a bug — it's pagination, a deliberate limit almost every real API has, and this lesson is about walking through every page of it correctly, without tripping the API's rate limit along the way.

per_page and page are the query parameters that control pagination. per_page equals 100 is GitHub's actual maximum per request, and page equals 2 would fetch the next hundred after that — but incrementing page by hand until you get an empty list back is the naive approach this lesson is about to improve on.

GitHub tells you directly whether there's a next page, in the response's Link header, and requests parses that for you into response.links — a dict keyed by relation name like next and last. The moment you're on the final page, next simply isn't in that dict anymore, and that's exactly the condition to loop on.

This loop walks every single page automatically: it extends one growing list with each page's results, follows response.links next when it's there, and sets url to None the moment it isn't. No hardcoded page count, no guessing how many contributors pandas actually has.

Every response carries rate-limit headers, and unauthenticated requests to GitHub are capped at 60 per hour per IP address — authenticating raises that to 5,000, but even that's a real ceiling a big pagination loop can hit. Go over it and you get a 403, not a crash, so a real pipeline checks X-RateLimit-Remaining before firing the next request instead of just hammering the API.

That's the whole chapter — files, CSV, JSON, exceptions, and real API calls with pagination. Chapter 4 starts right where this leaves off: you've got clean, real data pulled from a file or an API, and now it's time to load it into pandas Series and DataFrames.
